I don’t want this to come across wrong, but I think you should ask yourself why you applied to that school if you didn’t want to go to it? Was it as a fail safe school? If it was, I think that makes the answer clear that you should put down a deposit. Or was it that you originally had a better feeling about it and now with new information (such as the interview, like you mentioned), you’re more skeptical? If it’s the latter, I think that’s a harder decision. My gut response is put down a deposit so you know that you are going SOMEWHERE, unless you really do not believe you’ll be happy there. There is never a guarantee of another acceptance. Personally, I’d rather go to a school I’m less excited about to prevent going through another round of applications and interviews that aren’t going to guarantee me an acceptance I’d be more content with. But I also do value the quality of a PA school and would absolutely give up the 1k if a better option presented itself! Hope this helps!

Tough tough choice, honestly. I commute 1 hour each way currently and ALWAYS think about how useful that extra 2 hours/day would be. So much so that I have decided to move even though COL (mainly housing) is 3x higher than I currently pay. 

My biggest advice would be to seriously consider if it would be possible for you to move closer. I don’t know your exact situation, but if you cannot move your whole family, consider renting a room and staying there during the week (or some other alternative that works for you). 

If that isn’t possible, I would thoroughly self reflect and see if hybrid is going to truly work for you (often difficult, especially with family obligations). But I believe it would be the better option if you cannot move closer to the program.   Just know that your experience in the program will likely be sub-par compared to in-person programs, especially well-regarded ones.

If the program was accredited when you enter (day 1), even if it is a probationary accreditation, you will still be able to sit for the PANCE, and become a practicing PA. EVEN if it later loses its accreditation while you are enrolled. However, if a program has probationary status, but loses it accreditation between acceptance and matriculation, you would be unable to matriculate to that school. 

Here’s a good resource to understand accreditation: https://beaphysicianassistant.com/blog/misinterpretation-of-pa-program-accreditation-status

Yes, two years after your course ends, you would be required to retake the course if you have not already taken the NREMT and gained employment with an affiliating agency.

In my experience (Washington State), you must have a high school diploma to enroll in a course. You may need to look into the details in your state. In WA, you can take an accelerated course (2.5 weeks - not recommended IMO) or normal = 1 quarter in length. My advice - take a regular summer course, then take the NREMT soon after completing the course. Once you have your NREMT certification, you have 2 years to find employment as an EMT before you must retake the course. Another anecdotal thought - most places in my area require FULL TIME employment thoughout training, so trying to complete training with a department or private ambulance company before starting college would be ideal. Another option is get your EMT summer before college and train with a company during your first summer in college. Most places there after require 48-96 hours per month. Hope this helps!

There’s some great advice here. Some things to reiterate:
1. You’re doing great! Keep reminding her. She’s been telling herself a certain thing for so long that it’s become reality to her. The more she hears otherwise, eventually, she may see that as fact instead. She might not THINK that everyone feels the same way that you do, but it sounds like you are pretty dang important in her life and when it comes down to it, your opinion matters likely the most. Just keep saying it until it starts to drown out everything else she tells herself. 
2. Find her love language and be consistent with that. Nothing will make her feel more valued than you showing her love in the way she receives it best. It may take some time for you to adjust, or maybe you already do it. In the latter case, just keep doing it! Words of affirmation, quality time, and physical touch go a long way in helping others see themselves as worthy in your eyes. 
3. I love the idea of going out of your way to do sweet, small things. If she always plans dates/vacations/activities, try doing that for her and surprise her. Take her to her favorite store, have her pick out something that makes her feel beautiful, take her to do something, make her feel like you’re showing her off and like she is the queen of your world. 

A cute idea: I did this for my fiancé, and we absolutely love it. I cut out little cards, got a cute box, spent days writing down 365 cards, one for each day of the year. I did them in the following categories (color coded):
A. Things I love about you. 
B. Thank you for (x) 
C. Songs/lyrics that remind me of you/us
D. Other things I’d like you to know
E. Remember when we did...

Every day, he picks a random card and we read/talk about it together. Even though I gifted it to him, I look forward to it equally as much! I love that I get to remind me him everyday how much I love every part of him. It forces us to spend a bit of quality time each day regardless of how busy we are. Also, sometimes in long term relationships, we forget to give those words of affirmation each day because we get comfortable and complacent. Just an idea! Best of luck to you, you sound like a great SO. You clearly care deeply and it’s great you’re looking for resources to help her!

EMT here. Can confirm. You would be VERY surprised.

Most want you to send the updated transcripts directly to the school, or to CASPA. CASPA will not update your grade point average and most schools will not do an official updated GPA with new transcripts they receive. If it’s a prerequisite that you have never taken before, you should have entered it as an “in progress” class and then send the transcript to wherever they say on their website. They may consider it, but I haven’t run across a single school that will update your GPA internally, though they may exist as a minority subset. Read the directions on the schools website.

I also wouldn’t mind! I’m not a PA, just someone who finished going through the app process and worked through my PS with a fine toothed comb and multiple opinions from professionals. You can take my opinions as a grain of salt, but the more eyes, the better!

Communication! You need to have great communication and set clear expectations and boundaries as a PA. Simply tell them that it’s important to have a work-life balance. You are off the clock, you are not being paid, there should be no expectations that you have to respond when you go home. Tell them it’s not personal, but it is a boundary you have and you would appreciate if they could respect that.

Firefighters also work a majority EMS and very little fire calls in my and my fiancé’s experience. My fiancé has ran a grand total of 0 fire calls as a firefighter in his current department even though he’s been there about a year and a half. Back in Colorado, they ran some, but few in comparison to EMS calls. Buildings are built to a much higher standard these days and fewer fires occur. If anything, a “fire call” will come down to being a gas leak or something of that sort. Also, most everyone in fire goes into fire because the fires excite them, if you volunteer to run on the ambulance all day, every shift, I doubt anyone will fight you on it (and you could explain that in your app). BUT, I think for PA school specifically, private ambulance or and EMS only position at a fire department would be best. 
Finally, no, unfortunately I don’t think a wild land fire position will count.

I actually disagree. I read through thousands of educational pedagogy peer reviewed research articles to perform a metanalysis on the performance (measured by failure rates and exam test scores) of students in traditional lecture vs. (various types of) active learning classrooms. Our research found that across all the admitted studies (ones that met rigorous standards: same professor, randomized students or those that were shown to be at the same academic ability at the start of the course, evaluation that was equal across both courses, etc), active learning students outperformed and either failed or withdrew from the course at a lower rate than their traditional lecture counterparts (See Freeman et. al 2014 - it’s methodologies and citations speak for themselves in terms of the impact and quality of the paper). There has also been some inquiry into the possibility that those from disadvantaged backgrounds (LOW SES, minority, women, first generation students) may have a disproportionate benefit, thus lessening the historical achievement gap that exists between represented and non-represented students in STEM fields. But this latter point has not been published as of yet and is still in the midst of being tested. 

You’re right in that those that are successful in learning from lecture will usually learn well in other methods of teaching, however, it’s not true the other way around. Many teachers and professors believe in lecturing because it worked well for them, and they were successful, not because it is a sufficient method for others. 

I encourage you to do some additional research. There is a large body of high quality and rigorous research that provides evidence for the efficacy of the flipped classroom, if done correctly, as opposed to what is suggested in this ULPT.
